newsitem.title: democratic republic of congo: DEMOCRACY PROTEST BEFORE KABILA INAUGURATION.
newsitem.headline: DEMOCRACY PROTEST BEFORE KABILA INAUGURATION.

text.p: Hundreds of students calling for democracy and payment of grants protested in Kinshasa's main sports stadium on Thursday ahead of the inauguration there of self-proclaimed president Laurent Kabila.
Some members of the crowd took up the chant for democracy in the Democratic Republic of Congo, formerly Zaire. Soldiers led some students away. Others, elsewhere in the stadium, chanted sporadically.
State television commentators played down the protest, describing it a natural part of student life and saying it added to festival atmosphere.
At least 30,000 Kinshasa residents turned out to catch their first glimpse of Kabila, whose forces marched into the capital on May 17 after a seven-month civil war.

State television and airport sources said the presidents of Uganda, Rwanda, Angola, Burundi and Zambia had arrived to attend the inauguration of Kabila, who has kept out of the public eye since arriving in Kinshasa on May 20.
Mobutu's former military band serenaded the crowd.

"We automatically have unconditional respect for the head of state," Major Kawamonoko Ngodia, commander of the 250-strong brass band, told Reuters. "It does not matter who it is. Before it was Mobutu, now it is President Kabila."
Others were less complimentary. An unemployed computer programmer said neighbouring powers were telling Kabila what to do. "Kabila has sold out the country," he said.

The government declared Thursday a public holiday in the city and state radio urged the population to turn out in force at the Chinese-built stadium, formerly named Kamanyola after Mobutu's most famous battle against an early revolt.
The stadium holds upwards of 80,000 people.
"Today is an historic day for our country," the radio said.
Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo has banned political activity and public demonstrations, citing the need to preserve public order.

On Wednesday, he decreed himself sweeping powers to run the country until the adoption of a new transitional constitution by a promised constituent council. Earlier in the day, his soldiers broke up a third opposition protest in under a week.
Wednesday's 15-article decree, broadcast on state radio and television, said individual liberties would be guaranteed subject to respect of the law, public order and morals.
"The government conducts the policies of the nation as defined by the president," the decree added.

Mobutu ruled mineral-rich Zaire for over three decades, during which rampant corruption drained what is potentially one of Africa's richest nations. Foreign and domestic pressure forced him to abandon his near absolute powers in 1990 for a transition to democracy, but implementation dragged.

Several thousand supporters of Etienne Tshisekedi, a veteran Mobutu opponent, took part in Wednesday's march, denouncing the continued presence in Kinshasa of Rwandans among Kabila's forces and seeking power-sharing.

Kabila has set up a 13-member government. Aides say he plans to name seven more ministers but not a prime minister, the post Tshisekedi claims is constitutionally his after a 1992 national conference vote under Zaire's democratic transition.

Tshisekedi enjoys support in the capital's poor districts. His Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) has called another march for Friday. State radio announced a parallel march by supporters of Kabila.
Soldiers from Kabila's Alliance allowed Wednesday's march to go ahead but dispersed the protesters later, beating some.
"We will continue until there is an army in the service of the people," Tshisekedi ally Joseph Olenghankoy said, but he expressed the hope that Tshisekedi and Kabila would meet.
Opposition activists marched in Kinshasa last Friday and Saturday before the ban. Soldiers broke up those marches.
